basis: New mission, no workbook source; written per docs/plans/new-mission-playbook.md, angle distinct from sdg1 (general safety-net framing) and sdg1-3 (education/mobility framing): the labor market specifically. Facts and sources: minimum wage NT$29,500/month, NT$196/hour from 1 Jan 2026 (up from NT$28,590/NT$190 in 2025), 10th consecutive annual rise, cumulative +47.4% monthly/+63.3% hourly, 2.47 million workers benefiting (Ministry of Labor announcements via Taiwan News/Focus Taiwan, Sep-Dec 2025). OECD low-wage threshold ~NT$390,000/year; 1.26 million full-time employees (16.8%) below it in 2024; median regular monthly wage ~NT$37,000 (DGBAS 2024 wage statistics via Liberty Times). Atypical (part-time/temporary/dispatch) employment over 800,000 workers in 2024 (DGBAS Manpower Utilization Survey via 人間福報). Delivery riders ~88,000 by end of 2020, historically classified as contractors excluded from the Labor Standards Act; 2019 rider deaths triggered union push (Rest of World, New Bloom Magazine, GBLL). Delivery Workers Rights Protection and Delivery Platform Management Act: passed by Legislative Yuan 6 Jan 2026, promulgated 21 Jan 2026, effective 21 Jul 2026; NT$45/order floor rising with minimum wage, mandatory group accident insurance and liability insurance, deactivation appeal process (Legislative Yuan, Ministry of Labor, CNA, Taipei Times, Jul 2026). Rev.2: split run-on sentences that blew past the 20-second cap, rebalanced long-word% into the B2 band (some slides were over-dense, one was under), and added concession/passive/participle-clause/cleft instances so B2 carries the grammar range a CEFR examiner expects, not just harder vocabulary.

slides.1: Imagine a student juggling lectures by day and delivering food orders by night, someone whose hours already accumulate into a full-time job. Working this hard, she still refuses to call her situation secure, and neither should we.
slides.2: SDG 1's mandate is to end poverty in every form, a goal most people associate with welfare payments and emergency shelters. This talk instead examines a group that is often overlooked: people who work hard and remain poor regardless.
slides.3: Since January 2026, Taiwan's minimum wage has stood at NT$29,500 monthly, equivalent to NT$196 hourly. For many students listening today, that number represents not an abstract statistic but the precise amount appearing on their own payslip.
slides.4: Taiwan calculates a low-wage threshold at two-thirds of the median wage, near NT$390,000 a year. In 2024, around 1.26 million employees were classified as low-wage earners, while the median monthly wage sat at about NT$37,000.
slides.5: A large share of Taiwan's workforce sits outside full-time work. By 2024, more than 800,000 people held part-time, temporary, or dispatch jobs, roles that rarely offer real job security.
slides.6: Food delivery riders illustrate this precarity clearly. By 2020, roughly 88,000 people were riding for Uber Eats or foodpanda, yet these platforms classified them as contractors for years, so riders were excluded from the Labor Standards Act.
slides.7: Genuine, measurable progress has occurred here. Taiwan has consistently raised its minimum wage for ten consecutive years, a trajectory that has lifted the monthly figure by 47.4% and the hourly figure by 63.3%.
slides.8: In January 2026, Taiwan enacted a new law: the Delivery Workers Rights Protection and Delivery Platform Management Act. It set NT$45 as the minimum per order, and insurance became required for every platform.
slides.9: Riders have moved from an unregulated arrangement, with no guaranteed pay and no mandatory insurance, to a legally protected one. That shift has already taken effect, since the act came into force in July 2026.
slides.10: Is further growth in the minimum wage actually sustainable? Narrowing the low-wage gap this way sounds appealing, although it may force smaller employers to compensate by cutting hours, staff, or both.
slides.11: Currently, only delivery riders benefit from this rule. Instead of limiting reform to one sector, lawmakers could extend a similar floor to other workers, who otherwise are left without any comparable guarantee.
slides.12: Other genuine solutions exist too, beyond new laws alone. Riders can organize together instead of negotiating alone, while atypical workers more broadly can join training programs that move them into stable, full-time jobs.
slides.13: Low and unstable pay reaches far beyond a bank balance. If young workers cannot accumulate savings, they will postpone moving out, marrying, or starting a family, decisions an entire generation is now delaying.
slides.14: However, large enterprises are not the only ones exposed here. A small noodle shop, operating on wafer-thin margins, faces a genuine threat from a higher wage bill or a new insurance cost, not merely an inconvenience.
slides.15: However, the new law protects delivery riders here, leaving a large group unprotected. A part-time cashier or a dispatch factory worker still remains without any guaranteed floor or real insurance.
slides.16: However, the consequences of this reach the whole country, not just individual households. What this really costs Taiwan is a demographic decline that grows harder to reverse with every delayed marriage and postponed child.
slides.17: Two truths coexist here: a decade of wage increases has genuinely paid off, and riders have finally secured real protection. Yet a much larger group of atypical workers is still left waiting for anything comparable.
slides.18: This is not an abstract policy debate for someone else entirely. Many students in this room are already working part-time jobs or delivering food between lectures, which makes this story theirs as much as anyone's.
slides.19: Investigating the current minimum wage yourself is the first step. Should your pay or your delivery app fall short of it, you are entitled to question why, and equally entitled to ask about your insurance coverage.
slides.20: Sufficiency, not mere survival, ought to be what a wage guarantees. Real, measurable progress has occurred, although the underlying work is far from complete, and it starts by interrogating the very job in front of you.
